About General Compute
General Compute is a neocloud that rents out AI inference capacity built on specialized chips from Nvidia rivals such as SambaNova, Cerebras, Positron AI and d-Matrix. It buys the hardware and runs it in rented colocation data centers, using Nvidia GPUs to process prompts and the specialized chips to generate output tokens faster. General Compute makes money by selling this capacity to AI companies and inference providers, either as dedicated bare-metal servers or as a guaranteed tokens-per-second service under one contract. The company finances its chip purchases partly with a debt facility of up to $400 million from Upper90 and expects its first large-scale deployments to go live in the first quarter of 2027.

Dream Labs Raises $90M Seed for Any-Robot AI Model [2026]
Tom Vance
Updated Nov 3, 2026 · 17 min read
Dream Labs, a San Francisco startup founded by former Nvidia robotics researchers, came out of stealth on October 19, 2026 and announced that it has raised $90 million in seed funding to build foundation models that can run on robotic hardware from almost any manufacturer. The round, led by B Capital with participation from Kindred Ventures, A.Capital, Unusual Ventures, SV Angel, Wing VC, Scribble VC, and angel investor Adrian Aoun, is one of the largest seed checks written this year for a company betting that robot “brains” should be decoupled from robot bodies.

Related Coverage
The announcement lands alongside the public debut of Dream API, which Unite.AI reports the company describes as the first commercially available API for a robot foundation model. According to the announcement, Dream API takes a robot’s camera feed plus a plain-English instruction and converts both into motor commands, including on hardware the underlying model has never seen before. For a hardware industry that has spent the past two years chasing custom silicon for AI inference, Dream Labs is making the opposite bet: that the bottleneck in robotics is not the chip inside the machine, it is the software brain that has to generalize across thousands of different chassis, grippers, and sensor rigs.

What Dream Labs Actually Announced
The core of the announcement is Dream-1, a robot foundation model that the company describes as a World Action Model that “controls robots it has never seen, performs tasks it was never shown, and runs from $3/hour,” trained on videos of people performing everyday tasks rather than on robot-specific teleoperation data alone. Dream Labs says the model can handle tabletop tasks such as picking and placing objects and folding laundry, and that it can control bimanual robots fitted with parallel grippers without needing robot-specific training beforehand. That claim, if it holds up under independent testing, is the whole pitch: one model, deployed through an API, working across hardware it was never explicitly tuned for.
